risks.title: Weak session handling enabling account takeover via mobile wallet
Frequent promotional rule changes causing customer-facing pricing inconsistencies
Open banking API rate limits impacting real-time balance updates
Biweekly release cadence outpacing regression test coverage
Marketing promotions not reviewed against consumer disclosure rules

narrative: A retail bank is refreshing its consumer mobile wallet app, adding tap-to-pay, spending-insights, and configurable in-app promotional offers. Primary users are retail customers; internal stakeholders include product management, UX, marketing, and engineering, who meet weekly and are broadly available for review. The approved requirement set is settled for the current release but several requirements note that promotional rules, pricing tiers, and UI experiments are expected to change often as marketing tests new offers. Releases are planned on a biweekly cadence to keep pace with these changes. The app integrates with the bank's core ledger, a card network, and an open banking API layer. Regulatory context covers consumer data protection and open banking disclosure rules, and a small number of requirements map to those standards. Security exposure centers on authentication and payment tokenization. Budget and schedule pressure are moderate, tied to a marketing campaign window rather than a hard external mandate. A failure would primarily affect customer engagement metrics and could trigger minor compliance findings around promotional disclosures, but would not threaten core banking operations.
title: NovaLedger Mobile Wallet Refresh

risks.title: Balance reconciliation mismatches between legacy core and bridge layer
Limited legacy vendor SME availability delaying defect resolution
Incomplete audit trail during dual-running period
Missed decommission date extending dual-running costs
Data mapping errors between legacy field formats and new schema
Elevated access rights required for bridge maintenance
Batch-to-real-time timing gaps causing stale balances

narrative: A regional bank is building an interim bridge layer connecting an aging mainframe core ledger to newer digital channel systems, ahead of a scheduled core decommission. Users are internal treasury, operations, and channel teams rather than end customers. The vendor subject-matter experts for the legacy core system are available only a few days per month, which has slowed clarification and review cycles and left a notable number of open questions. The approved requirement set is largely stable, driven by the fixed decommission timeline, though a meaningful share needed revision once legacy field mappings were understood in detail. Reconciliation between balances produced by the legacy core and the bridge layer is treated as critical, with dual sign-off required before any figures are trusted downstream. Regulatory context concerns the integrity of data feeding capital and liquidity reporting, with strong audit trail expectations. The project is large, heavily integration-dependent, and not expected to change much in scope once underway. Failure would mean balance discrepancies, reporting errors, regulator scrutiny, or a missed cutover date that extends costly dual-running.
title: Heritage Trust Core Migration Bridge

risks.title: Rapid pricing tier changes causing customer confusion
Disclosure language lagging behind fast product iteration
Small team capacity strain during peak campaign launch

narrative: A small innovation unit within a bank is building a lightweight origination flow for micro-loans aimed at underbanked customers, intended to launch alongside a marketing campaign with a fixed budget and date. The team is small, and all identified stakeholders, including the product owner, a compliance representative, and the engineering lead, were interviewed and remain highly available for ongoing questions. The approved requirement set is small and settled for launch, but several requirements note that loan limits and pricing tiers are expected to change frequently as the team learns from early performance data, and frequent releases are planned to support that iteration. Integration is limited to a credit bureau API and a bank account verification service, with no dependency on legacy core systems. Regulatory context involves standard lending disclosure rules, with light applicability given the small loan sizes involved. Verification needs are modest since transaction values are low. A failure here would mainly affect this product line's early adoption and reputation rather than the bank's broader operations, given the limited scale and blast radius.
title: QuickTier Micro-Loan Origination

risks.title: Underwriting rule misapplication triggering fair lending exposure
Legacy loan origination system interface instability
Appraisal vendor data delays affecting underwriting turnaround
Schedule pressure compressing user acceptance testing
Disclosure timing miscalculation for certain loan types
Title vendor integration data format mismatches

narrative: A large lender is rebuilding its mortgage underwriting workflow, integrating a legacy loan origination system with appraisal vendors, title providers, and multiple credit bureaus. Users span underwriters, compliance and legal staff, and loan officers. Stakeholders were mostly interviewed, though the domain's complexity meant several rounds of clarification were needed before requirements were approved. The requirement set is large and, once baked into mandated compliance rules, is not expected to change much during delivery. Regulatory context includes several mortgage lending regulations governing fair lending and disclosure timing, and a substantial share of requirements demand dual review of underwriting decisions and detailed audit trails to satisfy examiner expectations. Schedule pressure is tied to a mandated regulatory effective date rather than a marketing window, leaving limited room to slip. Verification needs are extensive given the financial and legal consequences of underwriting errors. Integration complexity is high across appraisal, title, and bureau systems, several of which are older interfaces with limited documentation. A failure would mean regulatory violations, mispriced loans, and significant reputational and financial exposure for the lender.
title: Meridian Mortgage Underwriting Platform

risks.title: Real-time payment message tampering in transit
Sanctions screening bypass under peak transaction load
Irrevocable payment errors during exception handling
Missed scheme certification deadline
Core banking integration latency breaching scheme SLAs
Dual control process bottleneck during high volume periods
Message format version mismatches with scheme network

narrative: A bank is building a new real-time payments gateway to connect to a national instant-payments scheme, integrating core banking, sanctions screening, and fraud-check services. Participation carries a hard external deadline set by the scheme operator, and stakeholders across payments operations, security, and compliance have made themselves highly available given the deadline pressure. The approved requirement set is large and integration-heavy, spanning many connected systems, though the core message-handling rules themselves are not expected to change much once finalized. Because payments made through the scheme are irrevocable once settled, a large share of requirements demand precise message-level verification, reconciliation, and dual control for exception handling before any transfer is released. Regulatory and security context is significant, covering sanctions screening obligations and exposure to real-time fraud. Frequent releases are planned during the run-up to launch to allow incremental testing against the scheme's certification environment. A failure would mean missed scheme certification, financial loss from erroneous irrevocable payments, and regulatory penalties tied to sanctions screening gaps.
title: SwiftRail Instant Payments Gateway

risks.title: Certification test failure delaying terminal rollout
Legacy POS controller compatibility issues
Field technician training gaps at rollout

narrative: A merchant-acquiring unit is refreshing point-of-sale terminal software that connects to a legacy POS controller and card network switches. The scope is narrow and the dedicated team, all of whom were interviewed, is small and fully available throughout the project. The approved requirement set is stable, with very little revision needed and few recorded stakeholder conflicts, since the interfaces to the legacy POS controller are well documented and long established. The dominant concern is certification testing against payment card industry requirements rather than ongoing feature change; a large share of requirements demand exact verification against certification test scripts. Once certification is achieved, deployment frequency is expected to be low, limited to periodic maintenance releases rather than continuous delivery. Integration is limited to the legacy controller and existing card network switches. Regulatory context is narrow but strict, centered on certification standards for card payment acceptance. A failure would mean certification denial or transaction processing errors, with financial and reputational impact largely contained to this acquiring product line rather than the wider bank.
title: Coral POS Terminal Refresh

risks.title: Fraud pattern drift outpacing rule update cycle
Elevated false positive rate blocking legitimate transactions
Model scoring latency impacting checkout flow
Limited data science availability delaying rule tuning
Transaction feature data retained beyond policy

narrative: A bank is replacing a batch fraud-scoring process with a real-time transaction scoring service built around a rules and machine-learning pipeline. Fraud patterns are expected to shift frequently as fraud rings adapt their tactics, and several approved requirements explicitly state that rule thresholds and model parameters will need frequent, sometimes near-daily, updates once live. Frequent deployment of rule and model changes is planned to keep pace. Data science and fraud-operations stakeholders have limited availability for requirements review because of competing incident-response duties, which left a meaningful number of clarification questions unresolved at approval time. Integration spans the live transaction stream, case management tooling, and model-serving infrastructure. Regulatory context is comparatively light, since this is treated primarily as an internal risk control rather than a reporting obligation, though data retention practices are noted. The project is medium-sized. A failure could mean either undetected fraud losses if scoring lags behind evolving patterns, or excessive false positives that block legitimate customer transactions and damage trust.
title: SentryPulse Real-Time Fraud Scoring

risks.title: Missed suspicious activity report filing deadline
Legacy case system data migration errors
Four-eyes review bottleneck during alert spikes
Watchlist data handling exposure
Examiner findings requiring remediation plan
Watchlist feed integration delays

narrative: A bank is replacing its anti-money-laundering alert triage and case management tooling, integrating a legacy case system, sanctions and watchlist data, and core banking transaction feeds. Compliance and legal stakeholders are fully engaged and were all interviewed, given the regulatory stakes involved. The approved requirement set is large and stable, anchored closely to established suspicious activity reporting obligations, so little revision was needed and requirement volatility going forward is expected to be low. A substantial share of requirements demand four-eyes review of case evidence and thorough documentation to satisfy filing obligations and examiner audit expectations. Integration complexity is moderate, centered on the legacy case system and watchlist feeds rather than a wide range of external services. Regulatory context is significant, spanning suspicious activity reporting rules and examiner expectations for case handling. Delivery is not expected to be frequent once the system is live, as changes to case workflows go through a formal change process. A failure would mean missed suspicious activity reports, regulatory findings, or an examiner-mandated remediation program.
title: GuardLine AML Case Management

risks.title: Estimator inaccuracy causing claim over/under-payment
Imagery model bias across vehicle damage types
Repair-shop network data quality issues
Budget overrun from post-launch model tuning

narrative: An insurer is building an automated estimator for auto insurance claims that combines repair-shop network pricing data, imagery-based damage assessment, and lookups against an existing policy system. Budget is fixed by the annual claims-technology allocation, creating cost pressure on the delivery. Stakeholders, including claims operations, actuarial, IT, and a repair-network partner, were mostly interviewed, though a handful of clarification questions on damage-assessment edge cases remain open. Accuracy of generated estimates is central to the project, and a substantial share of requirements demand verification of automated estimates against manual adjuster figures during a phased rollout. Some further change is expected as damage-assessment models are tuned using post-launch performance data, and moderate release frequency is planned to support that tuning. Integration with the existing policy system is moderate in complexity. Regulatory context covers claims handling fairness expectations rather than a dense set of standards. A failure would mean over- or under-paid claims, customer dissatisfaction, and direct financial leakage for the insurer.
title: ClearPath Auto Claims Estimator

risks.title: Premium recalculation errors affecting large policyholder base
Missed annual renewal cutover date
Limited actuarial availability delaying review sign-off
Incomplete documentation for regulator review
Legacy policy admin data extraction errors
Reinsurance system data mapping inconsistencies

narrative: An insurer is building an annual policy renewal and premium recalculation module on top of a decades-old life policy administration system, with integration to an actuarial modeling system and a reinsurance platform. The actuarial team is based overseas with little overlapping working time with the delivery team, which has slowed clarification and review and left a substantial number of open questions at approval time. A fixed cutover date tied to the annual renewal cycle drives schedule pressure, since renewals for the full policy book must process on time. Requirements are largely stable, closely anchored to existing policy terms, though a notable share needed revision once legacy data extraction details were understood. Recalculated premiums are subject to extensive reconciliation requirements, and thorough documentation is needed to satisfy regulator and auditor review of the renewal process. Integration with the legacy policy administration system and reinsurance platform is central to the design. A failure would mean incorrect premiums charged at scale, a wave of policyholder complaints, regulatory findings, or a missed renewal cutover date.
title: Harbor Life Policy Admin Renewal

risks.title: Late regulatory filing due to reconciliation delays
General ledger reconciliation discrepancies
Dual sign-off bottleneck near filing deadline
Formula misinterpretation against regulator specification

narrative: A bank is building an automated liquidity coverage ratio report feeding directly into a mandated recurring regulatory filing, integrating a data warehouse, the treasury system, and a legacy general ledger. Requirements are highly stable, derived directly from a published regulatory formula, with almost no expected change over time and very few recorded conflicts. Treasury, finance, and compliance stakeholders form a small group, all of whom were interviewed and remain closely engaged given the recurring nature of the obligation. A large share of requirements demand exact reconciliation of report figures to the general ledger and dual sign-off before each filing is submitted, alongside thorough documentation of the calculation methodology. Fixed, recurring regulatory filing dates apply, creating steady rather than one-off schedule pressure. Integration with the legacy general ledger is a known, well-understood interface. The project is comparatively small in scope but carries high accuracy expectations given direct regulatory consequences. A failure would mean a late or inaccurate regulatory filing, drawing direct regulatory penalty and heightened scrutiny of the reporting function.
title: Beacon Liquidity Coverage Ratio Reporting

risks.title: Reporting breach across multiple regulator obligations
Source system feed failures affecting report completeness
Field-level reconciliation gaps against regulator-mandated format
Cross-regulator deadline conflicts straining delivery capacity
Exception-handling backlog during peak reporting periods
Legacy data feed format inconsistencies
Open compliance gaps pending regulator guidance
Stakeholder conflicts delaying rule finalization

narrative: A large financial institution is building a consolidated transaction-reporting platform that serves obligations to several distinct regulators simultaneously, aggregating feeds from many trading and payment source systems, including some older data feeds with limited documentation. Reporting rules change relatively often as regulators issue updates, so while a portion of the approved requirement set is stable, a substantial share needed revision during analysis and several conflicts were recorded between requirements favored by different business lines and different regulator liaisons. Stakeholders span multiple business lines and compliance functions, most of whom were interviewed, though clarification and open compliance gaps remain pending further regulator guidance. Extensive field-level reconciliation and exception-handling verification are required to ensure report accuracy, alongside heavy documentation obligations to support each regulator's audit expectations. Multiple fixed, non-negotiable regulatory deadlines apply across the different reporting streams, creating sustained schedule pressure throughout delivery. Integration complexity is very high given the number of source systems involved. A failure would mean reporting breaches across multiple regulators, financial penalties, and reputational damage.
title: Atlas Transaction Reporting Hub
